extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, rulewriters, administrative law practitioners, and policymakers concerned with notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for identifying, understanding, and responding to mass, malattributed, and computer-generated public comments in administrative rulemaking, including legal limits on what agencies may consider and practical processing concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mass comment response / mass comment campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'mass comment response' describes situations where agencies receive an unusually large number of comments (e.g., hundreds or thousands as opposed to a few dozen or fewer that are typical). No specific numeric threshold is defined; as a general matter, a mass comment response will feature at least an order of magnitude increase (e.g., 10x) in the number of comments received vis-à-vis a typical rulemaking for that agency. A 'mass comment campaign' is the special case where one or more organizations successfully urge many individuals to submit comments or submit comments in their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds vary by agency and rule; distinguish spontaneous mass responses from organized mass campaigns (which often produce identical or nearly identical language). Agencies should be aware that lower-cost electronic submissions make mass responses more frequent and duplicative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments are comments falsely attributed to persons by whom they were not in fact submitted (e.g., submitted under the name of someone who did not prepare, approve, or submit it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattribution is facilitated by easy access to large datasets of personal information and by automation; malattributed comments are related to but distinct from false substantive statements in comment bodies. Consideration of malattribution focuses on false identity rather than other falsehoods in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-generated comments are those generated by a software algorithm, replacing both human content generation and human interaction with the agency. Once automated, software can generate and submit comments (possibly repeatedly) without further human engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although early computer-generated comments have been crude and easy to detect, advances in NLP (e.g., GPT-3) mean machine-generated text can appear human-like and could in theory overwhelm agencies with human-quality comments. Not all computer-generated comments are harmful—some could provide technical assistance (e.g., identifying typos or broken links).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of information commenters provide (technical/operational vs. preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary types of information in comments: (1) technical/operational information (scientific/engineering studies, data, analysis about regulatory impacts and compliance), and (2) expressions of preference or conclusions about desirability of a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical/operational information facilitates higher-quality rulemakings; preference information's appropriateness is debated. Agencies often find technical information most useful, while preference information may matter when agencies must decide values left unresolved by statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and judicial limits on what information agencies may consider
rubrics_metrics.description: There are substantive limits on the kinds of information agencies may consider: under State Farm, an agency rule is arbitrary and capricious if the agency has relied on factors Congress did not intend it to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must ensure comments relied upon concern factors statutorily relevant to the rulemaking. Example: EPA cannot consider costs when setting NAAQS (Whitman v. American Trucking), so public preferences about costs are irrelevant in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality / significance threshold for which comments require agency response
rubrics_metrics.description: Only comments that, if true, raise points relevant to the agency's decision and that, if adopted, would require a change in the proposed rule, impose a duty on the agency to respond; purely speculative comments that do not disclose factual or policy bases require no response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (Home Box Office, Portland Cement, MCI WorldCom) articulate that agencies need not reply to every comment, only those that could be thought to challenge a fundamental premise or that are significant/material. An agency's failure to address comments is legally significant only if it shows the agency did not consider relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to respond in a reasoned manner to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must 'respond in a reasoned manner to the comments received, to explain how the agency resolved any significant problems raised by the comments, and to show how that resolution led the agency to the ultimate rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not required to address every submission, agencies must explain how they resolved significant issues and demonstrate that the final rule was based on consideration of relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance-over-volume principle ('the comment process is not a vote')
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and commentators emphasize that the number of comments received is generally less important than the substance of those comments; agencies are under no obligation to adopt the approach advocated by the largest number of commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts sometimes consider comment counts in non-rulemaking contexts, rulemaking review focuses on qualitative substance. Mass or form comments do not automatically carry decisive weight simply because of volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing and handling form comments
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general bar against agencies relying on form or identical letters; courts have upheld agency reliance on form letters where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may consider form submissions, including mass-solicited identical comments, but should assess their substantive relevance and, where necessary, seek to disentangle token/form responses from unique substantive input (for example, solicitations that ask for a brief personal sentence at the end).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness concerns in mass comment responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment responses raise difficult questions about the representativeness of the pool of commenters and the role of intermediary groups that conduct mass comment campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider how representative the commenters are of affected populations and weigh potential distortions introduced by organized campaigns versus spontaneous mass responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of extracting useful information from large volumes of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments can make it difficult to extract both technical/operational and preference information; useful technical information may be hard to find within a deluge of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies face challenges locating substantive input amid high volumes and duplicates; filtering and triage mechanisms may be necessary to surface actionable technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to identify and separate bot/malattributed comments to preserve preference information
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference information is only relevant to the extent it reflects genuine persons, making it necessary to separate out bot and malattributed comments from authentic submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should develop processes to detect non-human or falsely attributed submissions so that policy-relevant preference signals are not conflated with fabricated or automated inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and misinformation considerations in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is valuable only if accurate; false or erroneous statements in comments (intentional or otherwise) can delay, distract, or, if undiscovered, negatively affect a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies generally have expertise to recognize substantive errors and broad participation can counter misinformation, but agencies should remain vigilant about misinformation as an increasing concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing costs and resource implications of high comment volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing, analyzing, and responding to comments consumes time and resources; as the number of comments grows, processing costs increase, agencies may hire contractors, and time spent sorting out malattributed or computer-generated comments adds expense and delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should account for direct financial costs, staffing impacts, potential need for external contractors, and procedural delays when mass or automated comments occur; weigh processing burdens against informational and legitimacy benefits of public participation.
